models.collectorNote: This is the blue-chip summit of the French classics, provenance is researched chassis by chassis, and the atlas records the type, not individual cars.

generations.name: T150C / T150C-SS
generations.note: The SS (surprofilé) cars were the short-chassis sporting specials; racing T150Cs won the 1937 French Grand Prix's sports-car honours and placed at Le Mans.

models.intro: Anthony Lago's Talbot at its zenith: the T150C chassis with Wilson pre-selector gearbox and a 4.0-litre six, clothed by Figoni & Falaschi in the famous 'goutte d'eau' teardrop coupés, the most valuable French cars of the thirties, and regular concours Best-of-Show winners today.

models.collectorNote: Coachbuilt GS cars are individual works, value follows the body and its history. The Rosier Le Mans connection anchors the model's standing.

generations.name: T26 Record
generations.note: The Record's six was developed from the pre-war Grand Prix engine; saloon, coupé and cabriolet bodies were offered.

generations.name: T26 Grand Sport
generations.note: The GS shortened the chassis and raised the tune; Louis Rosier's 1950 Le Mans win was in a near-standard GS with a coupé body.

models.intro: Post-war Talbot-Lago: the 4.5-litre twin-cam six in the Record saloon and the short-chassis Grand Sport, one of the fastest road cars of its day and a Le Mans winner in 1950 (a T26 GS, father and son Rosier driving). Grand Sport chassis went to the great coachbuilders, Saoutchik, Figoni, Franay.

models.collectorNote: A footnote car with a fascinating spec sheet, buy on completeness, as trim and glass are effectively unobtainable off the shelf.

generations.name: T14 LS / America
generations.note: The BMW V8 cars made about 95 hp and are the majority of survivors; the four-cylinder cars are the purist's rarity.

models.intro: The last Talbot-Lago: a small coupé that began with Talbot's own 2.5-litre four and ended, as money ran out, with BMW's 2.6-litre V8 and the America name. About 120 were built; Simca bought the company in 1959 and the marque slept until the name resurfaced under Peugeot in 1979.
